top_story: By 13 June, U.S. and Iranian signals shifted from coercive brinkmanship toward a possible Sunday agreement, with Donald Trump tying any deal to the immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz after months in which Tehran had threatened wider regional escalation in response to U.S. pressure on its power grid. The diplomatic opening remained fragile because military action was still flaring near Hormuz as the talks advanced, showing that the waterway’s security is still being used as leverage rather than settled through stable de-escalation. This volatility sits alongside Gaza’s deepening humanitarian ruin, where slow recovery of bodies from the rubble is erasing identities as well as lives. The regional picture is therefore one in which headline diplomacy may ease a strategic chokepoint, but it does little to reverse the entrenched human devastation and coercive politics driving instability.
